name: Today's Report
headline: America's biggest builder expects fewer closings next year and says incentives are staying. Its Bay Area sale ends Sunday.
teaser: Today's theme is the builder's discount. D.R. Horton, the country's largest builder, reported Thursday that orders fell 7% last quarter and cancellations rose to 23% from 20%. It expects 79,000 to 84,000 closings next year, after 84,202 this year, and says incentives will stay elevated.

sections.label: Real estate
sections.html:
Today's theme is the builder's discount. D.R. Horton, the country's largest builder, reported Thursday that orders fell 7% last quarter and cancellations rose to 23% from 20%. It expects 79,000 to 84,000 closings next year, after 84,202 this year, and says incentives will stay elevated.

It reaches here. D.R. Horton's Red Tag sale, which it emailed local agents about this morning, covers Bay Area homes and ends Sunday. Nobody runs a Red Tag event when homes are selling themselves. On our own MLS, 33 of the 599 homes on the market in our five cities were built in 2025 or later, 20 of them townhomes, and they have been listed a median 52 days against 36 for older homes.

Rates got a small break. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average is 7.27%, from 7.29%, the lowest since late September and well below this month's 7.61% peak. The 15-year is 6.92%. The 30-year is still nearly a full point above a year ago, and this week's inflation report argues against counting on much more (see Economy).

One more new home item for Tuesday's ballot: California's Prop. 37 would let the state housing finance agency sell up to $25 billion in bonds to fund loans of up to 17% of the price for buyers of newly built homes who put at least 3% down and earn no more than double their area's typical income. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates no direct state or local costs.

The board wide table is 2,554, from 2,558, with 138 coming soon and 134 brand new. The five city ledger is 665, from 670: Fremont (223), Hayward (188) and Milpitas (101) eased, while Newark (90) and Union City (63) rose.

What this means for you: treat the builder's offer as the number to beat. Buyers looking at new homes should ask what the incentive is worth in rate and in price, then compare it with what a resale seller will give. Sellers of newer homes are up against that offer directly, so price against it, not against last spring.

  • Board wide: 2,554 listings across our 15 city table, counting active and in contract together, with 138 coming soon and 134 brand new.

Alameda County (Fremont Focus)

  • Live ledger: 665 listings across Fremont, Hayward, Milpitas, Newark and Union City. 599 are on the market and 66 are coming soon.
  • Fremont: 223 live, 173 active, 28 coming soon and 22 brand new. The median on market list price is $1,325,000 at $813 a square foot, and the typical active listing has been out 35 days.
  • The rest of the ledger: Hayward 188, Milpitas 101, Newark 90, Union City 63.
  • Across all five cities the median is $1,075,000 at $670 a square foot. 284 homes are priced under a million, and 178 have been sitting 60 days or longer.

sections.label: Economy
sections.html:
The economy is running hot, and for housing that matters more than any stock move. GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, and the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year ago. Core rose 0.3% and 3.1%. Hot growth and hot prices are what keep mortgage rates high, and two Fed officials dissented this week in favor of a hike. The next meeting is in December.

The 10-Year closed at 4.94%, from 4.98%, as stocks fell. Gold dropped to its lowest since early October 2025 and silver closed under $50 as traders weighed the risk of another hike. One correction: Market Briefs printed Thursday's 10-Year at 4.92% and Brent up 1.07% at $116.11; Treasury's close was 4.98%, and December Brent settled down 0.38% at $114.88.

sections.label: Stocks
sections.html:
A hard Friday, led by chips. Intel fell 28.6%, its worst day since at least 1980, after forecasting fourth quarter revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion when Wall Street expected about $17 billion. It is still up 78% this year, which shows how far the run had gone. Nvidia fell 4.2%.

Amazon is the other warning (chart). Over the past 12 months it took in $168.3 billion from operations and spent $210.7 billion on property and equipment, up $94.8 billion in a year, mainly for AI. That left free cash flow at negative $42.4 billion. The business itself is strong: AWS sales rose 39% and the operating margin hit a record 13.9%. After Alphabet's report this week, the question for every AI spender is the same: when does the cash come back?

Amazon's shares fell 1.41% Friday. Thursday's 4.25% drop came before its report, not after it, as Market Briefs implied.

images.alt: Bar chart of Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow from the first quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026
images.caption: Free cash flow fell from $25.9 billion to negative $42.4 billion in six quarters. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion, but spending on property and equipment rose faster, to $210.7 billion.

sections.label: Crypto
sections.html:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, suffered the biggest crypto hack on record Thursday. It puts the loss at about $6.3 billion, more than four times the old record of $1.5 billion at Bybit in 2025, says about $3 billion has been frozen, and says it will cover all losses. Bitcoin is down 4.12% over 24 hours, Ether 3.06% and XRP 1.64%, live from CoinGecko at 1:09 PM PT.

Coinbase fell 10.6% to $143.54 the day after its earnings and is now down 37% this year (chart). The newsletter's graphic said 28%, which was right through Wednesday. Most of its $719 million profit was gains on crypto it holds; adjusted net income was $78 million, and revenue fell 35% to $1.22 billion.

images.alt: Line chart of Coinbase month-end closing prices from December 31, 2025 to October 30, 2026
images.caption: Coinbase closed 2025 at $226.14 and closed October at $143.54, down 37%, after losing 10.6% on Friday.
